entities.name: Hen of the Woods / Maitake (Grifola frondosa)

plain_cards.back: Red Maple (Acer rubrum) — Opposite toothed 3–5 lobed leaf; red petioles; dominant Northeast wetland/upland deciduous tree.
plain_cards.attribution: The Cosmonaut · CC BY-SA 2.5 ca (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5 ca)

plain_cards.back: Sugar Maple (Acer saccharum) — Opposite 5-lobed leaf with smooth U-shaped sinuses (no fine teeth); source of maple syrup.
plain_cards.attribution: Superior National Forest · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Norway Maple (Acer platanoides) — Broad 5–7 pointed lobes; milky white sap when leaf stalk breaks; common invasive NYC street tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Silver Maple (Acer saccharinum) — Deeply cut 5-lobed opposite leaves with silvery-white undersides; fast-growing floodplain tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Boxelder (Acer negundo) — Only native Northeast maple with compound (3–5 leaflet) opposite leaves; green twigs.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern White Pine (Pinus strobus) — Only native Northeast pine with needles in bundles of 5 ('W-H-I-T-E'); feathery blue-green plumes.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Pitch Pine (Pinus rigida) — Twisted needles in bundles of 3 sprouting straight from dark scaly bark; Pine Barrens fire-adapted tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) — Flat lacy sprays of short blunt needles with two white stomatal stripes underneath; shade-tolerant ravine conifer.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Redcedar (Juniperus virginiana) — Scale-like foliage, fibrous peeling red-brown bark, and dusty blue berry-like cones; colonizes old fields.
plain_cards.attribution: USDA-NRCS PLANTS Database / Herman, D.E. et al. 1996. North Dakota tree handbook. USDA ... · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Balsam Fir (Abies balsamea) — Flat fragrant needles on smooth resin-blistered bark; upright cones; classic Northeast boreal conifer.
plain_cards.attribution: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Northern Red Oak (Quercus rubra) — Pointed bristle-tipped lobes (red oak group); flat saucer-like acorn cap; ski-track bark ridges.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: White Oak (Quercus alba) — Rounded bristle-free lobes; light ash-gray scaly bark; deep warty acorn cup; prized timber.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Pin Oak (Quercus palustris) — Deeply cut bristle-tipped lobes; lower branches droop down, middle horizontal, top upward; common NYC street tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Chestnut Oak (Quercus montana) — Deeply furrowed dark chunky bark; wavy scalloped margin leaves; dry Northeast ridgetops.
plain_cards.attribution: Bruce Kirchoff from Greensboro, NC, USA · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: American Sycamore (Platanus occidentalis) — Camouflage exfoliating bark (white, olive, brown); broad maple-like leaves; single fuzzy seed balls.
plain_cards.attribution: Lee Ann Ratledge · CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: London Plane (Platanus x acerifolia) — Hybrid sycamore dominant on NYC avenues; olive-cream flaking bark and seed balls hanging in PAIRS.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Paper Birch (Betula papyrifera) — Chalky white peeling bark with horizontal dark lenticels; cool northern woods.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Yellow Birch (Betula alleghaniensis) — Metallic bronze-gold curling papery bark; twigs smell strongly of wintergreen when scratched.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Sweet / Black Birch (Betula lenta) — Dark cherry-like smooth bark with horizontal lenticels; intense wintergreen-scented twigs.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: River Birch (Betula nigra) — Shaggy cinnamon-salmon peeling bark; heat-tolerant ornamental and streamside birch.
plain_cards.attribution: Photo by and (c)2016 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man) · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba) — Unmistakable fan-shaped leaf with dichotomous veins; living fossil ubiquitous as an NYC street tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: American Beech (Fagus grandifolia) — Smooth elephant-skin silver-gray bark; serrated parallel-veined leaves clinging tan through winter.
plain_cards.attribution: Photo by and (c)2016 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man) · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Tulip Tree (Liriodendron tulipifera) — Four-lobed cat-face leaf with flat notched tip; tallest straight-trunked Eastern hardwood.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: American Sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua) — Symmetric 5-pointed star leaf; corky twig wings; spiky woody 'gumball' fruits.
plain_cards.attribution: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma. · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Black Cherry (Prunus serotina) — Dark flaky 'burnt potato chip' bark; narrow finely toothed leaves with rusty hairs along midrib.
plain_cards.attribution: Gmihail at Serbian Wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 rs (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0 rs)

plain_cards.back: American Elm (Ulmus americana) — Graceful vase-shaped crown; lopsided doubly serrated sandpaper leaves; decimated by Dutch elm disease.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Honeylocust (Gleditsia triacanthos) — Airy bipinnately compound leaflets giving dappled shade; thornless cultivar dominates NYC sidewalks.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Black Locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) — Deeply braided rope-like bark; pinnately compound oval leaflets; ultra-rot-resistant fence-post wood.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Sassafras (Sassafras albidum) — Three distinct leaf shapes on one branch (oval, mitten, three-lobed); green citrus-scented twigs.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Shagbark Hickory (Carya ovata) — Long vertical curling plates of gray bark; 5-leaflet compound leaf with huge terminal leaflets.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Black Walnut (Juglans nigra) — Long pinnate leaves (15–23 leaflets); aromatic green husk nuts; chocolate-brown prized heartwood.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: White Ash (Fraxinus americana) — Diamond-patterned interlacing bark ridges; opposite compound leaves (7 leaflets); baseball bat wood.
plain_cards.attribution: Photo by and (c)2016 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man) · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Weeping Willow (Salix babylonica) — Long pendulous golden-green whip branches with narrow lance-shaped leaves; always near water.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) — Triangular heart-shaped leaves on flattened petioles that tremble in light wind; deep furrowed bark.
plain_cards.attribution: Matt Lavin from Bozeman, Montana, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Quaking Aspen (Populus tremuloides) — Chalky pale greenish-white bark with black eye knots; clonal root groves; round trembling leaves.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC0)

plain_cards.back: Flowering Dogwood (Cornus florida) — Opposite leaves with arcuate veins curving toward tip; 4 white notched bracts in spring; alligator-checkered bark.
plain_cards.attribution: Photo by and (c)2016 Derek Ramsey (Ram-Man) · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Redbud (Cercis canadensis) — Magenta pea-like blossoms erupting directly from bare spring branches (cauliflory); heart-shaped leaves.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: American Holly (Ilex opaca) — Broadleaf evergreen with stiff spiny matte green leaves and bright red winter berries on females.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima) — Huge compound leaves with glandular basal notch and burnt-peanut odor; invasive Brooklyn backyard weed-tree.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Bald Cypress (Taxodium distichum) — Deciduous conifer with soft feathery needles turning rust-orange in autumn; fluted buttress base and 'knees'.
plain_cards.attribution: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) — Broad-winged soaring raptor; dark belly band and rust-red upper tail; common over NYC parks and highways.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus) — Dark malar 'helmet' stripe, slate back, barred breast; fastest animal in a stoop (>300 km/h); nests on bridges.
plain_cards.attribution: slagheap from Canada · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: American Kestrel (Falco sparverius) — North America's smallest falcon; rusty back/tail, blue-gray wings on males, double black facial bars; hovers over fields.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Cooper's Hawk (Accipiter cooperii) — Long barred tail and short rounded wings for weaving through trees hunting songbirds; dark cap, fiery red eye.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) — White head and tail, massive yellow bill, 2 m flat-winged soar; winters along the Hudson River.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) — Fish-hunting raptor with crisp white underside, dark eye-stripe, and M-shaped crooked wings; huge stick nests on channel markers.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Great Horned Owl (Bubo virginianus) — Large powerful nocturnal owl with prominent ear tufts ('horns'), white throat bib, and deep 5-syllable hoot.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Barred Owl (Strix varia) — Round earless head, dark soulful eyes, vertical belly streaks; calls 'who cooks for you?'.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) — Tall slate-blue wading bird (~1.2 m) with S-curved neck in flight and yellow dagger bill.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Great Egret (Ardea alba) — Snow-white tall heron with yellow dagger bill and glossy black legs/feet.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) — Stocky hunched heron with black crown/back, pale gray wings, and ruby-red eyes; active at dusk in NYC parks.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Double-crested Cormorant (Nannopterum auritum) — Dark prehistoric-looking diving bird with hooked orange-throated bill; perches spreading wings to dry.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Canada Goose (Branta canadensis) — Black head and neck with white chinstrap; V-formation migrant and permanent urban park resident.
plain_cards.attribution: Image taken by Alan D. Wilson, and modified by Diliff (cropped and noise reduction appl... · CC BY-SA 2.5 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) — Iridescent green head, yellow bill, white neck ring on drake; mottled brown female with violet wing speculum.
plain_cards.attribution: This picture was realized by Richard Bartz by using a Canon EF 70-300mm f/4-5.6 IS USM ... · CC BY-SA 2.5 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Wood Duck (Aix sponsa) — Ornate crested male with emerald-violet head and crisp white facial stripes; nests in tree cavities.
plain_cards.attribution: Francis C. Franklin · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Herring Gull (Larus argentatus) — Large classic NYC coastal gull: pale gray mantle, black wingtips, pink legs, yellow bill with red spot.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) — Shaggy blue-gray crest, heavy dagger bill, rattling call; hovers then plunges headfirst for minnows.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Rock Pigeon (Columba livia) — Urban cliff-dweller descended from wild cliff doves; double black wing bars and iridescent neck sheen.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Mourning Dove (Zenaida macroura) — Sleek fawn-brown dove with pointed tail, whistling wingbeats on takeoff, and soft 'coo-OO-oo' song.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Downy Woodpecker (Dryobates pubescens) — Smallest North American woodpecker; crisp white back stripe, tiny stubby bill, red nape patch on male.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Red-bellied Woodpecker (Melanerpes carolinus) — Zebra-striped black-and-white back with bright crimson cap/nape (barely visible reddish belly blush).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Northern Flicker (Colaptes auratus) — Brown spotted ground-foraging ant-eating woodpecker; black chest crescent, white rump, golden-yellow underwings.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Pileated Woodpecker (Dryocopus pileatus) — Crow-sized forest woodpecker with flaming red triangular crest; chisels huge rectangular holes in dead timber.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Blue Jay (Cyanocitta cristata) — Crested cobalt-blue corvid with black necklace; caches acorns and mimics Red-tailed Hawk calls.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: American Crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) — All-black intelligent social corvid; squared fan tail and classic 'caw' (smaller than wedge-tailed Common Raven).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus) — Black cap and bib, crisp white cheeks; caches thousands of seeds and grows its hippocampus each autumn.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Tufted Titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor) — Mouse-gray songbird with pointed crest, big dark eyes, and peachy flanks; 'peter-peter-peter' call.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: White-breasted Nuthatch (Sitta carolinensis) — Blue-gray back, black cap, crisp white face; walks HEADFIRST down tree trunks probing bark crevices.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: American Robin (Turdus migratorius) — Large slate-backed thrush with warm brick-red breast; runs and pauses head-cocked on lawns listening for worms.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Gray Catbird (Dumetella carolinensis) — Sleek all-slate songbird with black cap and chestnut undertail; unmistakable cat-like 'mew' from dense shrubs.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Northern Mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos) — Long-tailed gray mimic flashing bold white wing patches; repeats each imitated phrase 3+ times.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: European Starling (Sturnus vulgaris) — Iridescent purple-green glossy bird speckled with cream in winter; introduced to Central Park in 1890; forms murmurations.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Cedar Waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) — Silky fawn-brown crested fruit-eater with sleek black bandit mask, yellow tail tip, and red waxy wing dots.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Yellow Warbler (Setophaga petechia) — Sun-bright all-yellow spring migrant with rufous chest streaks on male; 'sweet-sweet-sweet, I'm so sweet!'.
plain_cards.attribution: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Northern Cardinal (Cardinalis cardinalis) — Crested crimson male with black mask and heavy conical seed-cracking bill; year-round Northeast resident.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Red-winged Blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus) — Jet-black marsh male flashing scarlet-and-yellow shoulder epaulets; 'conk-la-ree!' over cattails.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Common Grackle (Quiscalus quiscula) — Long keel-tailed blackbird with piercing yellow eye and iridescent bronze-purple head.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: American Goldfinch (Spinus tristis) — Breeding male is electric lemon-yellow with black cap and wings; bouncy rollercoaster flight calling 'po-ta-to-chip'.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Dark-eyed Junco (Junco hyemalis) — Slate-gray hood/back, crisp white belly, pink bill, white outer tail feathers; classic Northeast winter 'snowbird'.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: White-throated Sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis) — Bold black-and-white head stripes, bright yellow lore spot, crisp white throat; sings 'Old Sam Peabody'.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Cumulonimbus — Towering convective storm cloud reaching the tropopause with an ice-crystal anvil top; lightning & downpours.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Cumulus Humilis (Fair-Weather Cumulus) — Flat-bottomed puffy cotton clouds wider than tall; marks gentle daytime thermal convection and fair weather.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.0 de)

plain_cards.back: Cumulus Congestus (Towering Cumulus) — Cauliflower-topped tall convective towers growing vertically; immediate precursor to thunderstorm cells.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Cirrus — High-altitude (>6 km) wispy ice-crystal filaments ('mares' tails'); often precede a warm front by 12–24 h.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Cirrostratus — Thin milky high-altitude ice veil covering the sky and producing a crisp 22° halo around the Sun or Moon.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Cirrocumulus — High-altitude tiny rippled white cloudlets without shading ('fine mackerel sky'); indicates upper-level instability.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Altocumulus — Mid-level (2–6 km) dappled gray-white rolls or patches with shaded undersides; signals mid-level instability.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Altostratus — Uniform blue-gray mid-level sheet dimming the Sun to a watery disk ('ground glass'); precedes steady rain.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Stratus — Low featureless gray blanket (<2 km) resembling elevated fog; brings mist or light drizzle.
plain_cards.attribution: Lee Ann Ratledge · CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Stratocumulus — Low lumpy gray-white cellular layer with blue breaks; most common cloud type over Earth's oceans.
plain_cards.attribution:
Another one of my pictures:



This photograph was taken by Medium69 (William Crochot) ... · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Nimbostratus — Thick dark featureless low-to-mid rain deck completely blocking the Sun; steady multi-hour precipitation.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Altocumulus Lenticularis — Stationary lens-shaped standing wave cloud formed downwind of terrain; signals strong winds aloft and rotor turbulence.
plain_cards.attribution: Dmitry A. Mottl · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Mammatus — Pouch-like cellular lobes hanging beneath a cumulonimbus anvil; formed by sinking cold moist air pockets.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Kelvin–Helmholtz Cloud (Fluctus) — Breaking-ocean-wave cloud curls formed by strong vertical wind shear between two air layers.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Arcus / Shelf Cloud — Low horizontal wedge attached to the leading edge of a thunderstorm outflow gust front; signals sudden wind surge.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Virga — Wispy streaks of rain or snow falling from a cloud base that evaporate before reaching dry ground.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Sundog (Parhelion) — Bright rainbow-tinted light spots 22° left and right of the Sun, refracted by horizontally aligned hexagonal ice plates.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Crepuscular Rays — Parallel shafts of sunlight streaming through cloud gaps that appear to fan outward due to linear perspective.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Belt of Venus / Alpenglow — Pinkish-peach twilight arch above Earth's dark slate-blue shadow opposite the rising or setting Sun.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Radiation Valley Fog — Clear calm nights let ground radiate heat away, cooling dense air below dew point into pooled valley fog.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Mica Schist — Foliated metamorphic rock sparkling with platy muscovite/biotite mica; bedrock beneath Midtown and Downtown Manhattan.
plain_cards.attribution: James St. John · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Granite — Coarse-grained felsic intrusive igneous rock: interlocking quartz, pink/white feldspar, and dark biotite/hornblende.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Columnar Basalt — Fine-grained dark mafic volcanic rock; hexagonal cooling joints (like the Palisades diabase sill across the Hudson).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Banded Gneiss — High-grade metamorphic rock with bold alternating light (quartz/feldspar) and dark (biotite/hornblende) mineral bands.
plain_cards.attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Siim assumed (based on copyright claims). · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Slate — Fine-grained low-grade metamorphic rock derived from shale; splits along crisp flat cleavage planes (roofing tile).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Marble — Metamorphosed limestone made of recrystallized interlocking calcite; soft (Mohs 3) and fizzes in weak acid.
plain_cards.attribution: The original uploader was Seth Ilys at English Wikipedia. · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Quartzite — Metamorphosed quartz sandstone fused so tightly it fractures cleanly across grains; ultra-hard (Mohs 7).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Cross-Bedded Sandstone — Clastic sedimentary rock of cemented sand grains; angled cross-beds preserve ancient dunes or river ripples.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Fossiliferous Limestone — Sedimentary rock mostly calcium carbonate (CaCO3) from marine shells/corals; forms karst caves and Portland cement.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Shale — Fine-grained laminated mudstone sedimentary rock; splits in thin flakes; major hydrocarbon source rock.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Conglomerate — Sedimentary rock composed of rounded river/beach pebbles cemented in a finer matrix (angular clasts = breccia).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Obsidian — Volcanic felsic glass cooled too fast for crystals; fractures with razor-sharp curved conchoidal ripples.
plain_cards.attribution: James St. John · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Pumice — Froth-filled vesicular volcanic glass full of trapped gas bubbles; low enough density (<1.0 g/cm³) to float on water.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Quartz Crystal (SiO2) — Hexagonal prismatic silicate crystal; Mohs hardness 7, glassy luster, conchoidal fracture, piezoelectric.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Pyrite (Fool's Gold, FeS2) — Brassy metallic isometric cubes with striated faces; harder (Mohs 6–6.5) and lighter than gold, greenish-black streak.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Potassium Feldspar (Orthoclase) — Most abundant mineral group in Earth's crust (~60%); salmon-pink/white blocks with two clean 90° cleavage planes (Mohs 6).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Calcite (CaCO3) — Rhombohedral carbonate crystal (Mohs 3) famous for optical double refraction and vigorous fizzing in acid.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Muscovite Mica — Silicate mineral with perfect basal cleavage peeling into flexible transparent silvery sheets.
plain_cards.attribution: Robert M. Lavinsky · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Glacial Erratic Boulder — Massive foreign boulder plucked and carried miles by Pleistocene ice sheets (ubiquitous across Central Park & Hudson Valley).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Glacial Striations — Parallel grooves scraped across exposed bedrock by rocks frozen into the base of advancing glaciers — shows ice flow direction.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron radicans) — 'Leaves of three, let it be'; shiny compound leaf with notched/mitten outer margins and hairy climbing vine; urushiol oil.
plain_cards.attribution: Agnieszka Kwiecień, Nova · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Virginia Creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia) — Harmless native vine with FIVE leaflets (often confused with 3-leaf poison ivy); turns brilliant crimson in autumn.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Staghorn Sumac (Rhus typhina) — Fuzzy antler-like twigs, long ferny compound leaves, and upright velvety crimson berry cones along Northeast roadsides.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Common Milkweed (Asclepias syriaca) — Thick opposite leaves oozing white latex, dusty-pink star flower umbels, warty seed pods; sole host plant of Monarch caterpillars.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Canada Goldenrod (Solidago canadensis) — Plumed late-summer yellow wildflower pollinated by insects (NOT the cause of hay fever — wind-pollinated ragweed is).
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Broadleaf Cattail (Typha latifolia) — Sword-like marsh blades topped by a dense velvety dark-brown cylindrical seed spike.
plain_cards.attribution: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Japanese Knotweed (Reynoutria japonica) — Bamboo-like hollow speckled stems, spade-shaped leaves; notoriously aggressive invasive rhizome cracking foundations.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Chicken of the Woods (Laetiporus sulphureus) — Bright sulfur-yellow and traffic-cone-orange overlapping shelf brackets on dead/dying oaks; choice edible polypore.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Hen of the Woods / Maitake (Grifola frondosa) — Frilly gray-brown rosette of overlapping caps fruiting at the base of mature oaks in autumn.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (Public domain)

plain_cards.back: Turkey Tail (Trametes versicolor) — Thin leathery fan brackets with concentric multicolored velvet zones and tiny white pores underneath; dead hardwood decomposer.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Yellow Morel (Morchella esculenta) — Honeycomb-pitted sponge cap completely HOLLOW from cap tip to stem base; prized spring woodland fungus.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Destroying Angel (Amanita bisporigera) — Pure ghostly white mushroom with cup-like basal volva, skirt ring, and white gills; contains lethal amatoxins.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Giant Puffball (Calvatia gigantea) — Soccer-ball-sized white globe fruiting in late-summer meadows; solid marshmallow-white inside when young.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Monarch Butterfly (Danaus plexippus) — Stained-glass orange wings with black veins and white-spotted borders; multi-generation 4,000 km migration to central Mexico.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail (Papilio glaucus) — Large lemon-yellow butterfly with bold black tiger stripes and hindwing tails; common Northeast summer butterfly.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Spotted Lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) — Invasive planthopper with polka-dotted tan forewings and flash-scarlet hindwings; favors Tree of Heaven and grapes.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Periodical Cicada (Magicicada) — Jet-black body, bulging ruby-red eyes, orange-veined wings; emerges synchronously every 13 or 17 years to swamp predators.
plain_cards.attribution: G. Edward Johnson · CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Bald-faced Hornet (Dolichovespula maculata) — Black-and-ivory aerial yellowjacket building basketball-sized gray paper nests hanging from tree limbs.
plain_cards.attribution: The High Fin Sperm Whale · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 3.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Gray Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) — Bushy-tailed scatter-hoarding rodent; ankle joints rotate 180° to descend tree trunks headfirst.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC0)

plain_cards.back: Raccoon (Procyon lotor) — Black bandit mask, ringed tail, hyper-sensitive hairless forepaws whose tactile acuity doubles when wet.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5)

plain_cards.back: Virginia Opossum (Didelphis virginiana) — North America's only marsupial; 50 teeth, prehensile tail, immune to most snake venom, eats thousands of ticks.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.5)

plain_cards.back: White-tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus) — Reddish-summer / gray-winter coat; flashes bright white underside of tail as an alarm flag when bounding.
plain_cards.attribution: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)

plain_cards.back: Red Fox (Vulpes vulpes) — Russet coat, black 'stocking' legs, white-tipped bushy tail; uses Earth's magnetic field to pounce on snow-buried voles.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 2.0)

plain_cards.back: Eastern Cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus) — Speckled brown-gray rabbit with rusty nape patch and powder-puff white tail; freezes motionless before zigzag sprinting.
plain_cards.source_note: Wikimedia Commons openly licensed photograph (CC BY-SA 4.0)
